title: Duleep returns to Sikhi, 1886
hook: stopped at Aden on his way to India, he takes amrit again

segments.voice: Yesterday, alahniyan, and your line was ashes carried home. Whose name did you say aloud? Today, her son tries to go home himself. Day nine hundred forty-five.

Officials climb aboard a steamer that has just tied up at a hot, rocky port, where ships bound for India stop to take on coal. They have orders for one of the passengers: he may go no further. The port is Aden. The passenger, traveling east with his family, is Duleep Singh. He has left England and set out for India, and he has told the Sikhs he is coming. He will never reach them. But in this port, something happens anyway. Today: Duleep returns to Sikhi.
screen: `A COALING PORT CALLED ADEN.` → `ORDERS: NO FURTHER.` → `SOMETHING HAPPENS ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: First, the turn. After his mother's stories, Duleep Singh began to read about the Sikh faith and about the annexation. He came to believe the terms that took his kingdom were unjust, and that the British owed him more than his allowance. He grew bitter, and he decided to go back to India and to the faith of his father. Second, the voyage. He set out by sea, and he wrote openly to the Sikhs that he was returning to them. The British government did not want him in India, where he might become a rallying point. So he was stopped at Aden. Third, the amrit. There, in a foreign port, Duleep Singh took amrit, the Khalsa initiation, from Sikhs who had come for it. The man who had been baptized a Christian as a boy was initiated as a Sikh as a grown man. He never reached the Punjab. But he had come back. Fourth, a song of joy addressed to a mother. In the Anand Sahib, Guru Amar Das opens with a cry of joy addressed to his mother: joy has come, mother, for I have found the true Guru. A mother who told her son who he was, and a son who came back to it, in the place where he was told he could go no further. And a look back at the week. bandhan, moh, the boy at Fatehgarh, the house in Suffolk, a mother found again and then lost. All week the story has moved away from the Punjab. Today, in the port where he was stopped, it turns toward it. That's today's line.
screen: `THE TURN TOWARD HOME.` · `STOPPED AT ADEN.` · `AMRIT IN A FOREIGN PORT.` · `JOY HAS COME, MOTHER.` · then, large: `HE CAME BACK.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with something you left. Sit, and let your breath settle. Bring to mind one thing you once loved and let go of: a practice, a language, a friend, a place, a habit of kindness. Don't judge yourself for leaving it. Just picture what coming back to it would look like, in the smallest possible way. One page. One phone call. One quiet minute. Breathe with that picture. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Amrit, the nectar of the Khalsa initiation: stopped at Aden on his way to India, Duleep Singh took it and came back to the faith of his father and mother. Today's word.
Your line: he came back. Today, take one small step back toward something you left, even if you can't go all the way. Day nine hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Sikhs take amrit, the Khalsa initiation, in a ceremony led by initiated Sikhs, and Duleep Singh's initiation at Aden is remembered as his return to the faith of his parents.

fork.setup: you're Duleep Singh. officials at Aden tell you you may go no further toward India. what do you do there, as the histories tell it?
options: give up and sail back to England quietly.
take amrit there, in the port.
slip away to India in disguise.
fork.reveal: he took amrit at Aden; he never reached the Punjab, but he had come back to Sikhi.

original.note: amrit, the nectar of the Khalsa initiation; taking amrit is how a Sikh joins the Khalsa.

trapdoor: what you thought: Duleep Singh went home to the Punjab.
what it means: he set out for India, was stopped at Aden, and took amrit there.
what a scholar hears: the British stopped him because they feared he would become a rallying point, and his return to Sikhi was bound up with his claims about the annexation.

notes: No year in the voice (the index title gives 1886). Week-end look back covers days 939–944.
Aden as a coaling port and the family traveling with him: confirm.

Editor: hook now opens on the officials' orders rather than a bare place name, and 'sold up in England' (unconfirmed) became 'left England'; the week's look-back no longer repeats day 938's 'something taken ... today, something kept' pattern.
Amrit 'from Sikhs who had come for it' (often linked to arrangements by Thakur Singh Sandhawalia): confirm who administered it.
Index hook says 'takes amrit again'; the voice says he took amrit (no prior initiation is established in this run). Confirm whether 'again' is accurate.
Anand Sahib pauri 1 (anand bhaiaa meree maae satguroo mai paaiaa) paraphrased; confirm Ang 917.
Audit: the Anand Sahib is a song of joy at finding the Guru, not a hymn 'about coming back'; the teach's framing line now says so.
